newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Labour closes gap on National Party --poll.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Labour closes gap on National Party --poll.

text.p: New Zealand's main opposition Labour Party has closed the gap sharply on the ruling National Party less than a week before a general election, according to a political opinion poll on Sunday.
The TVNZ poll showed support for the conservative National Party dropping six points to 34 percent, while support for Labour surged six to 24 percent.
The economic nationalist New Zealand First party was running neck-and-neck with the left-wing Alliance, both on 15 percent.
The poll follows another poll in Auckland-based newspaper The New Zealand Herald yesterday, showing support for Labour up six percent to almost 28, and National down 2.8 to 34 percent.

In the run-up to New Zealand's first election under a proportional voting system on October 12, both polls show that if the three main opposition parties were able to stitch together a coalition, they would have a clear majority.

The poll would give a Labour-New Zealand First-Alliance coalition 73 seats in a 120 seat parliament, and brings a Labour-NZ First or Labour-Alliance arrangement within striking distance of the 60 seats needed to command a majority in parliament.

National's potential coalition partners, the free-market ACT and the morals-based Christian Coalition, remained below the crucial five percent threshold at which parties who fail to gain a constituency seat qualify for proportional representation in parliament. Both gleaned only 3.8 percent support.

In the preferred Prime Minister stakes, National Party leader Jim Bolger received 23 percent support, while 17 percent of respondents favoured Labour leader Helen Clark. NZ First's Winston Peters was on 15 percent and Alliance leader Jim Anderton had 11 percent.

The poll comes a day before a second televised leaders' debate. Prime Minister Jim Bolger's poor performance in the first debate shook confidence in National's ranks, while boosting morale in the Labour camp as Helen Clark emerged the clear winner.
